1.pericope_label: These are also proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out: it is the glory of God to conceal a thing, but the honour of kings is to search out a matter: the heart of kings is unsearchable: take away the dross from the silver

schools.summary: Henry canvasses the question of who did the copying and leaves it open, whether the prophets living then, or men trained in their schools, or priests and Levites, or the princes and ministers of state, adding that if it was done by the officers remembered from that reign it was no diminution to their character; he observes that Christ is greater than Solomon here, since if all he said and did had been recorded the world could not contain the books; he adds that God’s way is in the sea so that we see what he does without knowing the reasons, and reports a reading that refers the concealment to the sins of men, since to cover sin is to pardon it; he requires of a prince that he search out matters himself and not judge hastily; and he makes wicked men the dross of a nation and the reformation of the court the way to the reformation of the kingdom.

Gill notes that some reckon a third and some a fourth part of the book to begin here, and takes the concealed things of the second verse as those God keeps to himself, the manner of what he does reveal remaining hidden.

Clarke reports that in his old manuscript Bible the first verse closes the preceding chapter, dates the collecting to about two hundred and seventy years after Solomon’s death, and argues that the men of Hezekiah may have been Isaiah and Shebna and others, since none but inspired men could have united such a supplement to the sacred book; he reads the concealment of the second verse as the manner in which God publishes his will, so that it must be seriously studied and is the more prized when discovered, and quotes a letter written to him by a royal correspondent on the divine origin of the sacred volumes; he reduces the unsearchable heart of kings to reasons of state which the common people cannot fathom; and he says no nation has a king for a public blessing till bad counsellors and sycophants are banished from the court. Wesley notes that many of these proverbs are political precepts which concerned Hezekiah and other princes in a special manner.

Keil and Delitzsch make Hezekiah the Jewish Pisistratos and his men the counterparts of the collectors employed to gather the poems of Homer, note that the abbreviated form of the king’s name does not favour deriving the title from the collectors themselves, and explain the verb rendered copied as meaning to snatch away or transfer, so that the question whence the proverbs were taken remains open, one rabbinic source answering from the Apocrypha and one modern scholar from the mouths of the people; they call the third verse a proverb that heaps up subjects before a single predicate and take its point to be a warning against the delusion of being flattered by a king’s favour; and they trace the words for separating and for the goldsmith who changes drossy metal by smelting. Ellicott supposes the proverbs had existed partly by oral tradition and partly in writing until Hezekiah had them copied into one collection, adds that we probably owe two books of the Psalter to the same care, says the further we search into nature or revelation the more depths appear, and renders the fourth verse as a vessel resulting to the refiner.

debates: Where did the men of Hezekiah get these proverbs? Keil and Delitzsch leave the question open, reporting one rabbinic answer that they came from the Apocrypha and one modern answer that they came from the mouths of the people; Ellicott supposes oral tradition and writing together; Clarke calls them traditionary sayings.

Who were the men of Hezekiah? Clarke names Isaiah and Shebna and holds that none but inspired men could have added such a supplement to the sacred book; Henry canvasses prophets, their scholars, priests and Levites, and princes of state, and refuses to decide.

What is concealed in the second verse? Gill and Wesley take it of God keeping his counsels in his own breast, Clarke of the manner in which revelation is published so that it must be studied, and Henry reports a further reading that refers it to the covering of sin in pardon.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch compare Hezekiah to Pisistratos and his men to the collectors of the poems of Homer.
Clarke interrupts his note on the second verse to quote a letter sent to him by a royal correspondent on the divine origin of the sacred volumes.
Ellicott credits the same king’s care with the compilation of two books of the Psalter as well as this collection of proverbs.
themes: a collection made two centuries later
what God keeps and what kings must find
a heart as unsearchable as the sky
favour that may be withdrawn unseen
the dross that must leave the court

5.pericope_label: Take away the wicked from before the king, and his throne shall be established in righteousness: put not forth thyself in the presence of the king: go not forth hastily to strive: debate thy cause with thy neighbour himself, and discover not a secret to another

schools.summary: Henry answers the charge that religion destroys good manners, since it teaches a man to behave lowly and reverently towards superiors and not to vie with them in apparel, furniture, gardens, housekeeping or retinue, which is an affront to them and a waste of his own estate; he presses past manners to self-denial, that a man be content in the sphere allotted him, and observes that this is in fact the way to advancement, as a parable of our Saviour that seems borrowed from this verse shows, while warning that modesty must not be pretended and made a stratagem for the courting of honour; and he says a man should not send for a writ in a passion, being apt to be partial in his own cause, but should weigh the certainty of the expense against the uncertainty of the success and first try to end the matter privately.

Gill assigns the parts of the refining figure, the wicked counsellors being the dross, the king the refiner and the kingdom the silver vessel that comes out the better for their removal; he keeps the sixth verse to the court, since a man should not appear too gay there or make a show above his station, princes not loving to be equalled and much less excelled; and he asks the questions that should precede a lawsuit, whether the cause is right, whether it will be thought frivolous and vexatious, and whether the man can bear the expense.

Clarke answers the sixth verse with eight lines of Ovid on Daedalus and Icarus, who had the same wings while the son flew aloft and the father skimmed the ground, and on the man who lives hidden living well; he calls the law a pit or bottomless deep to be kept from unless the direst necessity urges, observes that after a man has squandered his money on lawyers both they and the judge will leave the matter to twelve of his fellow citizens, and quotes from a well-known biography a list of eight things a man who goes to law should have, ending with good luck. Wesley reduces the sixth verse to not affecting familiar society with greater persons than oneself, and warns that the heat of contention must not provoke a man to divulge secrets committed to his trust.

Keil and Delitzsch render the sixth verse as a warning not to display oneself before the king nor approach the place of the great, who by descent and office hold a lofty place in court and state, and explain the reflexive verb as conducting oneself as a person of distinction; they leave two questions undecided at the eighth verse, whether the word for strife is an infinitive or a noun, and whether the going out is to the gate where justice was done or to the place where the adversary is met. Ellicott says violence and wrong pull a throne down where righteousness establishes it, points to the prince whose place a man has shamelessly taken, and offers two senses for the ninth verse, either the private dealing our Lord enjoins between a man and the brother who has trespassed against him or a rule against dragging others in by disclosing their secrets.

debates: Does the counsel about the king teach manners or morals? Henry takes it for both, first as reverence towards superiors and then as self-denial, and warns that humility must not be pretended as a stratagem for courting honour; Keil and Delitzsch keep to the court and the place of the great.
What should precede a lawsuit? Henry and Gill both require the cause to be weighed and the matter tried privately first; Clarke would keep from the law altogether unless the direst necessity urges.

Whose secret is not to be disclosed? Ellicott offers both the private dealing between a man and the brother who has wronged him and a rule against dragging third parties in, while Wesley warns against divulging secrets committed to one’s trust.
outliers: Clarke quotes eight lines of Ovid on Daedalus and Icarus, both furnished with the same wings, in support of living quietly below one’s fortune.
Clarke lists eight things a man who deliberates about going to law should have, the last of them good luck, and observes that lawyers and judge alike will end by leaving the matter to a jury.
Keil and Delitzsch leave open whether the going out of the eighth verse is to the court of justice or to the meeting with the adversary.
themes: the dross removed from the court
a place taken and given up again
wings that carried father and son differently
the certainty of expense, the uncertainty of success
a secret that is not yours to spend

10.pericope_label: Lest he that heareth it put thee to shame: a word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver: as an earring of gold, so is a wise reprover upon an obedient ear: as the cold of snow in the time of harvest, so is a faithful messenger: whoso boasteth himself of a false gift is like clouds and wind without rain

schools.summary: Henry offers golden balls resembling apples, or real apples of a golden colour, or gilded ones, set in a silver network basket or filigree box through which they could be seen, and supposes it some ornament of the table then well known; he says a reproof well given by a wise reprover and well taken by an obedient ear becomes them both; he takes the messenger rather than the drink, since the meanest servant owes faithfulness to the man who sent him and those who act for others by commission ought to act as carefully as for themselves; and he describes the boaster who raises expectations of what he will do for his country and what legacies he will leave, having either nothing to give or no intention of giving it.

Gill notes that either the man whose secret was told or the man it was told to may put the teller to shame; he renders the eleventh verse literally as a word spoken on its wheels, well circumstanced as to matter, method, time, place and persons; he observes that a golden earring gives pain when first put on and is ornamental only when well fixed; and he turns the false gift on teachers who boast of gifts they have not.

Clarke applies the word on its wheels to conversation, as coming in naturally and running smoothly, not forced nor dragged in and seeming to suit the whole company; he describes the silver filigree of the East at length, worked into flowers with joins scarcely perceptible, and says the golden fruit showing through it pleases the eye as the fruit pleases the palate in a sultry climate; he believes the ornament of the twelfth verse is a nose-ring with pendants, common in the East among women of condition; and he objects that stored snow could be had only by a few and not by labourers in a harvest field, preferring a coldness got by evaporation, since wine is cooled by wrapping the bottle in a wet cloth and hanging it in the sun. Wesley keeps to the golden apples showing through network of silver and to the empty clouds carried about with wind.

Keil and Delitzsch allow that the word of the twelfth verse elsewhere means a ring for the nose but hold that here it means an earring, as three old versions take it, and add a scholar’s argument that the word was dropped from later usage as an object used in idol worship; they make the pairing the point, since the two ornaments form one ensemble as a wise reprover and a hearing ear form a harmonious whole; they deny that a fall of snow is meant in the thirteenth verse, which in harvest would be a calamity, and make it drink cooled with snow fetched from the clefts of the mountains, noting that peasants near Damascus still store the winter’s snow and carry it down in the warm months; and they refuse for the fourteenth verse the sense of a worthless gift received and boasted of, since a lying promise obtains no gift at all, noting an Arabic word that means at once a boaster and a cloud that thunders much and rains little. Ellicott suggests pomegranates, citrons or oranges for the golden fruit and figured baskets for the pictures of silver, supposes the cooled drink familiar to a king with a summer palace in that country, and observes that clouds and wind commonly bring rain.

debates: Is the ornament of the twelfth verse an earring or a nose-ring? Keil and Delitzsch allow the second sense elsewhere but keep the earring here, with three old versions; Clarke holds for the nose-ring with pendants, which he says is common in the East among women of condition.

How was the drink of the thirteenth verse cooled? Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott describe snow stored in mountain clefts and carried down in summer; Clarke objects that this was beyond a harvest labourer and prefers cooling by evaporation, which he thinks removes all difficulty.
What is the false gift? Keil and Delitzsch refuse the sense of a worthless gift received and boasted of, since a lying promise obtains no gift at all, and keep it to a promise never performed.
outliers: Clarke describes Eastern silver filigree from his own observation, including animals made with every joint in natural play.
Keil and Delitzsch note an Arabic word that unites both halves of the fourteenth verse, meaning at once a boaster and a cloud that thunders much and rains little.
Clarke gives the method of cooling wine by wrapping the bottle in a wet cloth and hanging it in the sun, and prefers it to stored snow as the sense of the proverb.
themes: a secret that shames the teller
fruit seen through silver work
the ornament and the ear that hears
snow carried down from the clefts
clouds that promise and withhold

15.pericope_label: By long forbearing is a prince persuaded, and a soft tongue breaketh the bone: hast thou found honey? eat so much as is sufficient for thee: withdraw thy foot from thy neighbour’s house: a man that beareth false witness against his neighbour is a maul, and a sword, and a sharp arrow: confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble is like a broken tooth

schools.summary: Henry gives patience and mildness separately, the first to bear a present heat without being put into a heat by it and to wait for a fit opportunity, since what is just now will be just another time, the second a soft tongue that mollifies the roughest spirits like the lightning said to have broken a bone without piercing the flesh; he allows the honey as no forbidden fruit but warns that we are most in danger of surfeiting on what is sweetest; he makes it manners as well as wisdom not to visit too often, not to stay too long, not to come at meal-time and not to meddle in a family’s affairs, quoting two Latin tags and observing that God is a better friend, since we need not withdraw our foot from his house; he sorts the three weapons of the false witness by their range; and he gives both readings of the nineteenth verse.

Gill observes that a prince yields to mild representation and patient waiting what he would have rejected if it had been pressed with heat and haste, says a man should make his foot rare at a neighbour’s door, and offers both readings of the nineteenth verse, adding that the man who trusts his riches or his own righteousness is trusting what is deceitful.

Clarke sets the fifteenth verse beside the saying that a soft answer turns away wrath, extends the honey to all enjoyments, and says of the visit only that too much familiarity breeds contempt. Wesley takes the honey for all worldly delights.

Keil and Delitzsch say the man persuaded is a judge or holder of high office and that the verb means to win over rather than delude, since long-suffering makes it plain in the end that the accused has right on his side, boisterous passion injuring even a just cause; they call honey wholesome and therefore to be eaten sparingly, and collect a Greek line that honey taken immoderately is as bitter as gall and an old rhyme that its sweetness offends the man who takes too much; they quote an Arabic proverb that if your comrade eats honey you should not lick it all up, and observe that love between friends may turn to hatred through too much intercourse; they call the first line of the eighteenth verse a collection of instruments of murder with the second written under it as a subscription, since the false witness ruins his neighbour’s estate, takes away his honour and murders him; and they weigh and reject several proposals about the form of the word for broken in the nineteenth. Ellicott notes that finding honey was common where swarms of wild bees abounded in the woods, and glosses the maul as a hammer, connecting the word with the Latin and English names for a mallet.

debates: What is meant by the broken tooth? Henry and Gill both give two readings, the confidence of an unfaithful man, whose policy and interest fail him when trouble comes, and confidence placed in such a man, which fails under a weight and hurts while it fails.
Who is persuaded by long forbearing? Keil and Delitzsch make him a judge or holder of high office rather than a great person generally, and take the verb as winning him over rather than deluding him.

How far may honey be eaten? Keil and Delitzsch make it wholesome but to be taken sparingly, Henry warns that we surfeit soonest on what is sweetest, and Wesley and Clarke extend the rule to all delights.
outliers: Henry quotes two Latin tags on visiting, that after three days fish and company grow distasteful and that one should be too intimate with nobody, and adds that God is the better friend since we need not withdraw our foot from his house.
Keil and Delitzsch collect two sayings, one Greek and one in rhyme, to the effect that even honey turns bitter when too much of it is taken.
Keil and Delitzsch describe the first line of the eighteenth verse as a collection of instruments of murder with the second written beneath it as a subscription.
themes: patience that wins a hearing
a tongue soft enough to break bone
honey eaten by measure
a foot made rare at the door
a tooth that fails under weight

20.pericope_label: As he that taketh away a garment in cold weather, and as vinegar upon nitre, so is he that singeth songs to an heavy heart: if thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat: the north wind driveth away rain: it is better to dwell in the corner of the housetop than with a brawling woman

schools.summary: Henry says the sorrowful are to be comforted by sympathy, since it adds to their grief to see friends so little concerned and hardens them against the assaults of mirth, and notes a contrary reading by which songs of comfort refresh a mourner; he observes that the duty of loving enemies was an old commandment before our Saviour gave it fresh force by his own example, and that the way to turn an enemy into a friend is to act towards him in a friendly manner, mollifying him as a refiner melts metal by heaping coals upon it; he leaves the weather of the twenty-third verse for the moral, that slanders would not be so readily spoken if they were not readily heard and that we may reprove by our looks where we cannot otherwise; and he pities those unequally yoked, husband or wife alike, observing that those who live in solitude are at least free from the vexation of society.
Gill guards the coals of fire, which are not to increase the man’s punishment but to bring him to shame and repentance, and quotes a geographer for the swift north wind driving away the moist clouds.

Clarke gives the chemistry of the nitre, the natron of the ancients, carbonate of soda, found native as an efflorescence on the soil and in solution in certain lakes, named from a root meaning to dissolve since a solution of it takes out spots and is used in the East for washing; pour vinegar on it and a strong fermentation follows, which is his point, that between songs and a heavy heart there is no affinity and any attempt to unite them produces opposition and strife. He takes the coals of fire from smelting and quotes four lines of verse on the artist who melts sullen lead ore by heaping coals on its head until the pure silver runs below; and he prefers the marginal reading that the north wind brings forth rain, which he says holds at that city because the wind carries the vapours of the sea lying north of it. Wesley says the vinegar makes the nitre ineffectual.

Keil and Delitzsch say the three things of the twentieth verse are all wrong and the third morally so, since one ought to weep with those who weep, and report a scholar who found the difficulty in wearing a fine garment in severe cold; they commend the Greek rendering of the coals of fire, which an apostle cites, but refuse the common explanation that they stand for burning shame, since shame burns on the cheeks and not on the head; they derive the name of the north from a root meaning to conceal, from the darkening of the sky, but object that in that country the fathers of rain are the west and south-west, and note the substitutions by which older translators escaped the difficulty; and they observe that the twenty-fourth verse is a repetition. Ellicott says the vinegar renders the nitre useless, keeps the burning shame and adds that bringing a sinner to repentance pleases God, better than a resentment that usurps his prerogative of vengeance, and thinks the marginal reading of the north wind more correct while noting that some understand the north-west.

debates: Does the north wind bring rain or drive it away? Clarke prefers the marginal reading that it brings forth rain, with three versions in support though another reads the south wind; Ellicott agrees but notes an apparent contradiction and reports that some understand the north-west; Keil and Delitzsch object that the fathers of rain in that country are the west and south-west.

What do the coals of fire mean? Keil and Delitzsch refuse the common sense of burning shame, since shame burns on the cheeks and not on the head, and report two scholars who take it otherwise; Ellicott and Gill keep the shame, and Clarke and Henry make it a melting rather than a burning.

Should songs be sung to a heavy heart? All read the proverb as forbidding it, but Henry reports a contrary reading by which the garment warms and the vinegar dissolves, so that songs of comfort refresh the mourner.
outliers: Clarke gives a full chemical account of the nitre, its occurrence, its name and its use in washing, before applying the fermentation to the proverb.
Clarke quotes four lines of verse on smelting lead ore by heaping coals on its head until the pure silver runs below.
Henry observes that those who live in solitude, wanting the comfort of society, are at least free from its vexation.
themes: three things done at the wrong moment
no affinity between song and grief
coals that melt rather than burn
a wind that brings or clears the rain
a corner of the housetop

25.pericope_label: As cold waters to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country: a righteous man falling down before the wicked is as a troubled fountain: it is not good to eat much honey, so for men to search their own glory is not glory: he that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down and without walls

schools.summary: Henry allows the desire for news but checks it, since bad news will come too soon and good news is welcome whenever it comes, and turns the figure upward to heaven as a country afar off; he distinguishes three ways in which a righteous man falls before the wicked, by sinning where they can see it, by being oppressed and thrust into obscurity, and by turning cowardly and giving way, and finds all three a troubling of the fountains; he makes the twenty-seventh verse two deaths to die, to the pleasures of sense and to the praise of man, while reporting the other reading by which searching into glorious things cannot be excessive; and he sets out the man who governs his own thoughts and resentments against the man whose walls are down, out of whom all good goes and into whom all evil breaks.

Gill makes the thirsty man a traveller in hot countries where a spring is rarely met with, says simply that too much of anything is bad, and describes the man without rule as setting no guard and no fence about his passions.

Clarke quotes two old English versions of the twenty-seventh verse, both making the man who will search out high things find them too heavy for him, concludes that he who searches too far into mysteries is likely to be confounded by them, and then refuses to puzzle himself or his reader with the discordant explanations that have been brought forward. Wesley says good news is welcome because it comes rarely and with difficulty after long expectation, makes the oppression of righteous men a public calamity like the corrupting of public fountains, and calls the industrious seeking of applause not only sinful but shameful.

Keil and Delitzsch note that the word for thirsty properly means to be darkened, and so to faint, of the darkness that spreads over the eyes; they compare the righteous to a well for the blessing that flows from him to those around and allow that his yielding may be either forced or spontaneous, most interpreters thinking of compulsion; they declare the twenty-seventh verse scarcely to be understood as it stands and canvass four renderings, rejecting them all; and they explain the broken city as one whose wall is breached or wholly down and so incapable of defence, like a man who cannot hold his desires in check. Ellicott says the proverb about good news suggests how little communication passed in old times between distant countries, makes the yielding righteous man a fountain fouled by the feet of cattle since he can no longer counsel out of a pure heart, calls the sense of the twenty-seventh verse very doubtful while offering that searching into difficult matters may be an honour, and says the man without rule is exposed to the assault of every temptation.

debates: What does the twenty-seventh verse mean? Keil and Delitzsch call it scarcely intelligible and reject four proposed renderings; Ellicott calls the sense very doubtful and offers that searching into difficult matters may be an honour; Clarke declines to rehearse the discordant explanations at all; Henry keeps the received sense but reports the other.

Is the righteous man’s fall forced or willing? Keil and Delitzsch allow both and note that most interpreters think of compulsion, one taking it of a man driven from his dwelling; Henry distinguishes falling into sin, being oppressed, and giving way through cowardice; Ellicott takes the third.
Why is good news from far away so refreshing? Ellicott and Wesley both ground it in the rarity of communication between distant countries in old times.
outliers: Clarke breaks off his note on the twenty-seventh verse by refusing to puzzle himself or his reader with the discordant explanations of it that have been offered.
Ellicott makes the yielding righteous man a fountain fouled by the feet of the cattle that drink at it.
Henry turns the far country into heaven, from which good news reaches us in the gospel.
themes: news that has travelled far
a spring that others drink from
a verse nobody can construe
honey and applause together
walls that no longer stand
